name: message-translator
intent: Convert a message from one data format into another at the integration seam, so that systems with different data models or wire contracts can exchange messages without either side having to learn the other's representation.
problem: Two systems that must exchange messages disagree on format - field names, structure, units, encodings, what is optional - and neither can be changed (legacy systems, packaged applications, external partners). Without an explicit translation step every consumer parses and reinterprets the producer's format, both models leak across the boundary, and each new pair of systems multiplies the parsing code.
context: Integration boundaries between applications that each own a proprietary data model, or between an internal model and a standardised external format (EDIFACT, RosettaNet, a partner API). It applies wherever messages cross a seam that neither side can move - legacy adapters, EDI gateways, protocol bridges, published partner interfaces - and the source-to-target mapping therefore has to live in a component of its own, wired between the two channels.
benefits: Neither system changes: the translation is localised at the boundary, so a legacy or external application keeps its own model.
Neither side needs to know the other's model - only the translator embeds both schemas, and they stay out of both cores.
Format changes become local: adapting to a new wire version or partner dialect is an edit inside the translator instead of a coordinated release of both systems.
Translation is a natural checkpoint: validation and normalisation of dates, units, currency and encodings happen before the data reaches domain code.

With a canonical data model between several translators the number of mappings grows with the number of formats (two per participant) instead of with the number of pairs - the EIP catalog counts 30 pairwise translators for six applications against 12 with a canonical model.
A stateless translator is cheap to test with captured golden messages and is safe to retry, because the same input always produces the same output.
tradeoffs: Every translator is a permanent maintenance surface: a change on either side of the seam has to be re-expressed in the mapping code, and an unowned mapping rots silently while still passing traffic.
Pairwise translation grows quadratically; a canonical model fixes the growth but adds a second translation hop, more latency, and a model that must itself be governed.
Mapping is lossy wherever the models differ in semantics (attributes the target has no home for), so the translator must decide explicitly what to drop - a business decision hidden in technical code.
The seam costs a parse and a serialise: allocation, encoding and number/date precision issues that can dominate the cost of a small message, plus a hop that no debugger shows you.
A defective translator fails globally and silently: it corrupts every message on its path, and the damage is noticed downstream, far from the mapping code.
It attracts scope creep - validation, enrichment and orchestration rules accumulate in the mapping code until the translator is an undeclared business layer with no owner.

participants.responsibility: The filter component at the seam: consumes a message in the source format and emits the corresponding message in the target format. It owns both schemas and the mapping between them, and nothing else.
The wire or document representation produced by the sending system, with its field names, structure, units and encodings.
The representation the receiving system expects - its canonical or proprietary model, including the fields the sender cannot supply.
The rule set (mapping table, annotations, code or schema mapping) that pairs source fields with target fields and defines value-level conversions, defaults and drops.
The message channel the translator consumes from; it carries the source format, optionally signalled by a format indicator or datatype channel.
The channel the translated message is published to; it carries the target format and decouples the translator from its consumers.
Where messages that cannot be translated (unknown version, failed validation, missing field) are routed instead of being passed on or dropped in silence.

use_cases: Legacy integration: a fixed-width mainframe record or COBOL copybook file is translated into the JSON contract of a modern service.
B2B/EDI: an internal order model is translated into EDIFACT/X12 (or a partner-specific XML dialect) and the inbound acknowledgements back.
Versioned public API: v1 requests and responses are translated to v2 so existing clients keep working during a migration.
Protocol bridging: a JSON message consumed from a queue is translated into an Avro or Protobuf record for a different broker or stream processor.
Anti-corruption layer: data arriving from a SaaS/CRM model is translated into the internal domain model so vendor field names never reach the core.
Normalisation at the edge: dates, units, currency and character encodings are converted to the internal conventions before domain logic runs.
Format migration with coexistence: old and new formats run side by side during a staged rollout, one translator per direction and a deprecation date.
Apache Camel route: Camel's Message Translator EIP uses a transform or setBody step, a bean or processor, a template, or marshal/unmarshal data formats to adapt a payload between endpoints.
Spring Integration flow: a transformer endpoint converts payloads between producers and consumers, using an @Transformer method or the IntegrationFlow transform() DSL operator.
WSO2 Integrator: Micro Integrator's Message Translator/Data Mapper converts a client payload to the backend service's schema before invoking the backend endpoint.
avoid_when: The two sides can simply agree on one format - changing the producer once is cheaper than maintaining a translator forever.

Only key names differ and the framework already has a switch for it: serde's rename_all, a JSONDecoder keyDecodingStrategy, a struct tag or an alias option expresses the mapping with no new component.
The receiver can be changed instead: move it to the producer's model rather than living between two permanent formats.
The decision is routing rather than translation (which format or version is this message?) - that is a Format Indicator plus a Content-Based Router.

The change is enrichment (adding data the sender never had) or reduction (dropping unneeded fields): those are Content Enricher and Content Filter concerns that may sit next to, but not inside, the translator.
The seam is an in-process call between two objects of the same model - that is an ordinary Adapter, not a message-format boundary.
anti_patterns: The universal translator: one component mapping every format to every other, with n^2 branches; split it per pair or insert a canonical model.
Field-name shuffling without semantics: renames that ignore units, encodings, time zones and number formats, so the message looks right and is wrong.
Silent lossy translation: the target has no home for some source fields and the mapping drops them without a policy, a log or an alert.
The translator as business layer: routing, enrichment and business rules accumulate in the mapping code until nobody owns it.
Dual-shape 'universal' messages carrying both models with presence flags, re-coupling exactly the systems the translator was meant to decouple.
Hand-built target bytes: emitting XML/JSON by string concatenation or templates instead of a serializer, inviting escaping and injection defects.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: translation is its own responsibility; enrichment, routing and orchestration belong to their own patterns.
Boundary control and information hiding: the foreign schema never enters the domain model (the anti-corruption principle).
Open/closed for formats: a new format arrives as a new translator, not as a new branch in every consumer.
Dependency inversion: domain code depends on its own model; only the adapter depends on the foreign model.
Fail fast with an explicit invalid-message path instead of emitting a partly translated message.
best_practices: Keep the mapping total and explicit: every source field is either mapped or deliberately dropped, and the drop is logged or rejected rather than silent.
Express the mapping as data where possible (tables, annotations, schema mapping) so it can be reviewed and tested independently of code.
Introduce a canonical data model once more than two formats or participants are involved, and keep each translator one-directional: source in, canonical out.
Version the mapping with the message schema, tolerate unknown additions on the receiving side (Tolerant Reader) while staying strict about what the mapping consumes.
Test with golden messages captured from the real producers, including the lossy, the partially populated and the malformed cases; assert the failure path as hard as the happy path.
Keep the translator stateless and idempotent so redelivery is safe; inject code lists and clocks instead of reading globals.
Log the inbound and outbound shape under the same correlation identifier so the hop can be reconstructed when a receiver reports bad data.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Message Translator, in the Message Transformation chapter: a special filter between other filters or applications that translates one data format into another, the messaging equivalent of the Adapter pattern.
